items.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: I loved playing with him. ... I went there, and the nucleus of the Composers Workshop was there, and that’s the way Mingus’ Jazz Workshop records came into play.

ctx.x: Was there a noticeable difference at the time between let’s say the bands like Glenn Miller and the white oriented bands and Basie and Ellington that you can talk about?

Well there certainly was. A good example would be Dixieland music. I never realized until I made a study, I wanted to do a New Orleans concert at the school after being there for twenty-five years and never having seen one at Berklee, I guess it was a modern school for that time, I decided to do a New Orleans concert. And the students really loved it because it was so different from what they heard there. But in the process of preparing for it, I got to realize that the thing about feeling music in four-four…

evident qualities. Of course I had problems playing with white groups because my influences were black when I was young. When I first started hearing records around the age of sixteen, seventeen, I got into Lester Young and Duke and you know their music. Whenever I went to a white session and sat in, of course they were playing Dixieland music, and they’d accuse me of playing wrong notes and everything else, it was what I heard. And then I’d play in a black session and nobody seemed to be bugged about the…
Yeah, I assumed so, yeah, yeah. I have to listen to that again. Did you have any problem with -- that band was only partially a jazz band, wasn't it?
Yeah. Art Farmer, John LaPorta Porter --
